title: The password hashes are unsalted MD5
summary: A migration to bcrypt was started, reverted for a latency number, and never picked up again.

brief.subject: Auth review — I need a second pair of eyes before I write this up
brief.body:
Hello,

I am three days into the pre-certification review of the auth path and I want someone who knows this codebase to confirm what I think I am reading, before it goes in a report with your company’s name on it.

There is a note in the repository describing a migration that was started and then reverted. What I cannot tell from the outside is whether the revert left anything behind, or whether the 214,000 rows it mentions are still in the state the note implies.

This is not an active incident. Nobody is in your systems that I know of. That tends to make these easier to postpone, so I would rather we were both precise about what is true.

One thing I will need for the report: whether anyone raised this at the time, and what happened to it.

Yusuf
objectives: Confirm how a password is turned into what is stored in the database
Work out what an attacker holding a copy of the users table could actually do
Decide what a real migration costs, including the part nobody wants to pay

debrief.rootCause: Passwords are hashed with a single pass of MD5 and no salt, and the stored value is compared directly against a fresh hash of the submitted password. A migration to bcrypt was written and then reverted because the cost factor added latency to the login endpoint before a release, leaving `needsRehash()` behind as the only surviving piece. Every account created since — and every account that existed before — still holds the old format.
debrief.businessImpact: MD5 is designed to be fast, which is the opposite of what a password hash is for: commodity hardware tries billions of candidates per second. Without a salt, every user with the same password has the same stored value, so a single precomputed table cracks the common passwords across all 214,000 accounts at once rather than one account at a time. Anyone who obtains a copy of the users table — a backup, a read-replica, an SQL injection elsewhere in the product — effectively obtains the passwords themselves, and with them whatever else those passwords open.
debrief.remediation: Move to a memory-hard KDF such as argon2id or bcrypt with a per-user salt, and do it in two parts. Rehash on next successful login, which quietly converts active users at the moment their plaintext password is in hand, and set a deadline after which accounts still on the old format are forced through a reset. The latency that caused the revert is the algorithm working as designed; if the instances cannot carry it, the answer is the instance size or the cost factor tuned with measurements, not a hash with no work factor at all.

files.code:
# Auth migration — status

## Done
- `needsRehash()` helper added to password.service.ts
- Column widened to varchar(120) so a bcrypt hash fits

## Reverted 2026-06-02
Rolling new sign-ups onto bcrypt doubled p95 on /auth/login in staging
(cost factor 12 on the small instances). Reverted ahead of the spring release
so the number would not show up in the launch metrics. Ticket AUTH-418 raised
to revisit "after the release".

## Not started
- Rehash-on-login for existing users
- Anything about the 214,000 rows still holding the old hashes

questions.prompt: Which line decides how a password is stored?

options.text: password.service.ts line 4 — a single unsalted MD5 pass produces the stored value
password.service.ts line 8 — the comparison uses === rather than a constant-time equality
user.service.ts lines 23-27 — register inserts the hash with a parameterised query
password.service.ts line 12 — needsRehash decides the format from the string length

questions.explanation: Line 4 is the whole of the storage decision: one MD5 pass, no salt, no work factor. Line 8 is a fair thing to notice and worth fixing, but a timing comparison against a hash the attacker cannot influence is a much smaller problem, and it stops mattering entirely once line 4 is right. Line 12 is a leftover from the reverted migration rather than a defect.
hints: Follow what `register` eventually writes into the database.
One line turns a password into the string that is stored. Everything else moves that string around.
Look at what is passed to createHash, and at what is not passed to it at all.

questions.prompt: Why is an unsalted MD5 hash of a password not meaningfully better than storing the password itself?

options.text: MD5 has known collisions, so an attacker can sign in with a different string that hashes to the same value
MD5 is reversible, so the original password can be computed directly from the digest
MD5 is fast by design and the missing salt makes one precomputed table work against every account at once, so the digest is a thin delay rather than a protection
MD5 produces only 128 bits, which is too short to represent a long password without loss

questions.explanation: A password hash is supposed to be slow: the work factor is the defence, and MD5 has none, so an ordinary GPU tries billions of candidates a second. The missing salt is the multiplier — identical passwords produce identical digests, so the attacker cracks the population rather than the person, and "password123" falls once for everyone who chose it. Collisions do exist in MD5 but are not how this gets attacked, and the digest is not reversible in the sense option B describes; it does not need to be.
hints: Ask what property a password hash is supposed to have that a checksum is not.
Two users choose the same password. Compare what is stored for each of them.

questions.prompt: What does a real fix look like for the 214,000 accounts already stored this way?

options.text: Switch new registrations to argon2id and leave existing rows alone until those users happen to change their password
Add a per-user salt to the existing MD5 scheme, which removes the shared-table problem without the latency cost
Re-hash the stored MD5 digests with argon2id in a batch job, so no user has to do anything
Rehash on next successful login, set a deadline, and force a reset for the accounts still on the old format when it passes

questions.explanation: The plaintext password is only available at the moment someone signs in, which is why rehash-on-login is the mechanism — it converts active users invisibly. It is also why it cannot be the whole plan: dormant accounts never log in, and they are the ones most likely to be holding a reused password nobody has touched in years, so a deadline and a forced reset are the rest of it. Option C sounds attractive and is the trap: argon2id over an MD5 digest protects the digest, and an attacker who cracks the digest still has the password. Option B keeps a hash with no work factor.
hints: At what single moment does the server actually hold the user’s real password?
That mechanism handles the users who come back. Who does it not handle?
One option hashes the hash. Ask what an attacker has to recover for that to fail.

ethicalChoices.text: Tell Yusuf exactly what is stored, say in the report that it was raised in June and reverted for a launch metric, and commit to the migration with a forced-reset deadline even though it lands in the same quarter as the next release.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The report was uncomfortable to read and the certification went through with a remediation deadline attached. The migration took six weeks; rehash-on-login converted about 70% of accounts without anyone noticing, and the forced reset for the rest cost roughly 9,000 support contacts and a visible dip in weekly actives for a fortnight. The revert being named in the report is what got the work resourced, and your engineering manager said as much when the deadline was set.

ethicalChoices.text: Confirm the technical finding, but describe the June work as "deprioritised" rather than reverted for a launch metric, and propose switching new registrations to argon2id now with the backfill to follow later.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The report read as a team that had simply not got to it yet, and the remediation deadline came out generous. New registrations moved to argon2id. The backfill was scheduled twice and slipped twice, because nothing in the system was visibly broken. Fourteen months later a read-replica snapshot in a misconfigured bucket put the old hashes in someone else’s hands, and the incident review found the June ticket, the revert reason, and your wording. The finding was about the wording.

ethicalChoices.text: Give Yusuf the full technical picture, including the revert and why, and leave the decision about whether to fund the migration to the people who reverted it in June.
ethicalChoices.outcome: The report was accurate, which mattered: the external record now said what was true. Internally the migration went back into the backlog behind the release, roughly where it had been in June, and the same latency argument was made again by the same people. It was eventually done, eleven months later, after a customer’s own security questionnaire asked directly. Nothing was concealed. Nothing moved either, until somebody outside the company applied the pressure you had decided was not yours to apply.
